entries.be734e0896a5e2e54fdefc0709e130ed2aeb1295: <div sID="gen5351" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="1Sam.7" sID="1Sam.7"/> <div eID="gen5351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5352" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5353" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The eclipsing of the glory of the ark, by its privacy in Kirjath-jearim for many years, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1-1Sam.7.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The appearing of the glory of Samuel in his public services for the good of Israel, to whom he was raised up to be a judge, and he was the last that bore that character. This chapter gives us all the account we have of him when he was in the prime of his time; for what we had before was in his childhood (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1-1Sam.3.21">ch. ii. and iii.</reference>); what we have of him after was in his old age, <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.1">ch. viii. 1</reference>. We have him here active, 1. In the reformation of Israel from their idolatry, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3-1Sam.7.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. 2. In the reviving of religion among them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5-1Sam.7.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. 3. In praying for them against the invading Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.7-1Sam.7.9">ver. 7-9</reference>), over whom God, in answer to his prayer, gave them a glorious victory, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10-1Sam.7.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. 4. In erecting a thankful memorial of that victory, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.12">ver. 12</reference>. 5. In the improvement of that victory, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13-1Sam.7.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. 6. In the administration of justice, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.15-1Sam.7.17">ver. 15-17</reference>. And these were the things for which God was preparing the designing him, in the early vouchsafements of his grace to him.
entries.2feff65e75b9aeb39e8a83dd8bd21d9b92a3c419: <div eID="gen5353" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5352" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Ark at Kirjath-jearim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1099.)</title> <div sID="gen5354" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the men of Kirjath-jearim came, and fetched up the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill, and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> And it came to pass, while the ark abode in Kirjath-jearim, that the time was long; for it was twenty years: and all the house of Israel lamented after the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen5354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5355" type="x-p"/> Here we must attend the ark to Kirjath-jearim, and then leave it there, to hear not a word more of it except once (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.18">ch. xiv. 18</reference>), till David fetched it thence, about forty years after, <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">1 Chron. xiii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen5355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5356" type="x-p"/> I. We are very willing to attend it thither, for the men of Beth-shemesh have by their own folly made that a burden which might have been a blessing; and gladly would we see it among those to whom it will be a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life,</hi> for in every place where it has been of late it has been a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death.</hi> Now, <div eID="gen5356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5357" type="x-p"/> 1. The men of Kirjath-jearim cheerfully bring it among them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1">v. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">They came,</hi> at the first word, <hi type="italic">and fetched up the ark of the Lord.</hi> Their neighbours the Beth-shemites, were not more glad to get rid of it than they were to receive it, knowing very well that what slaughter the ark had made at Beth-shemesh was not an act of arbitrary power, but of necessary justice, and those that suffered by it must blame themselves, not the ark; we may depend upon the word which God hath said (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">Jer. xxv. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt.</hi> Note, The judgments of God on those who profane his ordinances should not make us afraid of the ordinances, but of profaning them and making an ill use of them. <div eID="gen5357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5358" type="x-p"/> 2. They carefully provided for its decent entertainment among them, as a welcome guest, with true affection, and, as an honourable guest, with respect and reverence. <div eID="gen5358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5359" type="x-p"/> (1.) They provided a proper place to receive it. They had no public building to adorn with it, but they lodged it in the house of Abinadab, which stood upon the highest ground, and, probably, was the best house in their city; or perhaps the master of it was the most eminent man they had for piety, and best affected to the ark. The men of Beth-shemesh left it exposed upon a stone in the open field, and, though it was a city of priests, none of them received it into his house; but the men of Kirjath-jearim, though common Israelites, gave it house-room, and no doubt the best-furnished room in the house to which it was brought. Note, [1.] God will find out a resting-place for his ark; if some thrust it from them, yet the hearts of others shall be inclined to receive it. [2.] It is no new thing for God's ark to be thrust into a private house. Christ and his apostles preached from house to house when they could not have public places at command. [3.] Sometimes priests are shamed and out-done in religion by common Israelites. <div eID="gen5359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5360" type="x-p"/> (2.) They provided a proper person to attend it: <hi type="italic">They sanctified Eleazar his son to keep it;</hi> not the father, either because he was aged and infirm, or because he had the affairs of his house and family to attend, from which they would not take him off. But the son, who, it is probable, was a very pious devout young man, and zealously affected towards the best things. His business was to keep the ark, not only from being seized by malicious Philistines, but from being touched or looked into by too curious Israelites. He was to keep the room clean and decent in which the ark was, that, though it was in an obscure place, it might no look like a neglected thing, which no man looked after. It does not appear that this Eleazar was of the tribe of Levi, much less of the house of Aaron, nor was it needful that he should, for here was no altar either for sacrifice or incense, only we may suppose that some devout Israelites would come and pray before the ark, and those that did so he was there ready to attend and assist. For this purpose they sanctified him, that is, by his own consent, they obliged him to make this his business, and to give a constant attendance to it; they set him apart for it in the name of all their citizens. This was irregular, but was excusable because of the present distress. When the ark has but recently come out of captivity we cannot expect it to be on a sudden in its usual solemnity, but must take things as they are, and make the best of them. <div eID="gen5360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5361" type="x-p"/> II. Yet we are very loth to leave it here, wishing it well at Shiloh again, but that is made desolate (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.14">Jer. vii. 14</reference>), or at least wishing it at Nob, or Gibeon, or wherever the tabernacle and the altars are; but, it seems, it must lie by the way for want of some public-spirited men to bring it to its proper place. 1. The time of its continuance here was long, very long, above forty years it lay in these fields of the wood, a remote, obscure, private place, unfrequented and almost unregarded (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The time that the ark abode in Kirjath-jearim was long,</hi> even till David fetched it thence. It was very strange that all the time that Samuel governed the ark was never brought to its place in the holy of holies, an evidence of the decay of holy zeal among them. God suffered it to be so, to punish them for their neglect of the ark when it was in its place and to show that the great stress which the institution laid upon the ark was but typical of Christ, and those <hi type="italic">good things to come which cannot be moved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">Heb. ix. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">xii. 27</reference>. It was a just reproach to the priests that one not of their order was sanctified to keep the ark. 2. Twenty years of this time had passed before the house of Israel was sensible of the want of the ark. The Septuagint read it somewhat more clearly than we do; <hi type="italic">and it was twenty years, and</hi> (that is, when) <hi type="italic">the whole house of Israel looked up again after the Lord.</hi> So long the ark remained in obscurity, and the Israelites were not sensible of the inconvenience, nor ever made any enquiry after it, what has become of it; though, while it was absent from the tabernacle, the token of God's special presence was wanting, nor could they keep the day of atonement as it should be kept. They were content with the altars without the ark; so easily can formal professors rest satisfied in a round of external performances, without any tokens of God's presence or acceptance. But at length they bethought themselves, and began to lament after the lord, stirred up to it, it is probable, by the preaching of Samuel, with which an extraordinary working of the Spirit of God set in. A general disposition to repentance and reformation now appears throughout all Israel, and they begin to <hi type="italic">look unto him whom they had slighted, and to mourn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zech. xii. 10</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot thinks this was a matter and time as remarkable as almost any we read of in scripture; and that the great conversion, <reference osisRef="Acts.2">Acts 2</reference> and 3, is the only parallel to it. Note, (1.) Those that know how to value God's ordinances cannot but reckon it a very lamentable thing to want them. (2.) True repentance and conversion begin in lamenting after the Lord; we must be sensible that by sin we have provoked him to withdraw and are undone if we continue in a state of distance from him, and be restless till we have recovered his favour and obtained his gracious returns. It was better with the Israelites when they wanted the ark, and were lamenting after it, than when they had the ark, and were prying into it, or priding themselves in it. Better see people longing in the scarcity of the means of grace than loathing in the abundance of them.
entries.19aba31b6150cf41a30991c7a6cce746d2c2864a: <div eID="gen5361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5362" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> And Samuel spake unto all the house of Israel, saying, If ye do return unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with all your hearts, <hi type="italic">then</hi> put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and serve him only: and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> only. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Samuel said, Gather all Israel to Mizpeh, and I will pray for you unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> And they gathered together to Mizpeh, and drew water, and poured <hi type="italic">it</hi> out before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and fasted on that day, and said there, We have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . And Samuel judged the children of Israel in Mizpeh. <div eID="gen5362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5363" type="x-p"/> We may well wonder where Samuel was and what he was doing all this while, for we have not had him so much as named till now, since <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1">ch. iv. 1</reference>, not as if he were unconcerned, but his labours among his people are not mentioned till there appears the fruit of them. When he perceived that they began to <hi type="italic">lament after the Lord</hi> he struck while the iron was hot, and two things he endeavoured to do for them, as a faithful servant of God and a faithful friend to the Israel of God:— <div eID="gen5363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5364" type="x-p"/> I. He endeavoured to separate between them and their idols, for <hi type="italic">there</hi> reformation must begin. He <hi type="italic">spoke to all the house of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">v. 3</reference>), going, as it should seem, from place to place, an itinerant preacher (for we find not that they were gathered together till <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">v. 5</reference>), and wherever he came this was his exhortation, "<hi type="italic">If you do indeed return to the Lord,</hi> as you seem inclined to do, by your lamentations for your departure from him and his from you, then know, 1. That you must renounce and abandon your idols, <hi type="italic">put away the strange gods,</hi> for your God will admit no rival; put them away from you, each one from himself, nay, and put them <hi type="italic">from among you,</hi> do what you can, in your places, to rid them out of the country. Put away Baalim, the strange gods, and Ashtaroth, the strange goddesses," for such also they had. Or Ashtaroth is particularly named because it was the best-beloved idol, and that which they were most wedded to. Note, True repentance strikes at the darling sin, and will with a peculiar zeal and resolution put away that, the sin which most <hi type="italic">easily besets us.</hi> 2. "That you must make a solemn business of returning to God, and do it with a serious consideration and a stedfast resolution, for both are included in <hi type="italic">preparing the heart,</hi> directing, disposing, establishing, the heart unto the Lord. 3. That you must be wholly for God, for him and no other, <hi type="italic">serve him only,</hi> else you do not serve him at all so as to please him. 4. That this is the only way and a sure way to prosperity and deliverance. Take this course, and <hi type="italic">he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines;</hi> for it was because you forsook him and served other gods that he delivered you into their hands." This was the purport of Samuel's preaching, and it had a wonderfully good effect (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They put away Baalim and Ashtaroth,</hi> not only quitted the worship of them, but destroyed their images, demolished their altars, and quite abandoned them. <hi type="italic">What have we to do any more with idols?</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">Hos. xiv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa. xxx. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen5364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5365" type="x-p"/> II. He endeavoured to engage them for ever to God and his service. Now that he had them in a good mind he did all he could to keep them in it. <div eID="gen5365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5366" type="x-p"/> 1. He summons all Israel, at least by their elders, as their representatives, to meet him at Mizpeh (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">v. 5</reference>), and there he promises to pray for them. And it was worth while for them to come from the remotest part of the country to join with Samuel in seeking God's favour. Note, Ministers should pray for those to whom they preach, that God by his grace would make the preaching effectual. And, when we come together in religious assemblies, we must remember that it is as much our business there to join in public prayers as it is to hear a sermon. He would pray for them that, by the grace of God, they might be parted from their idols, and that then, by the providence of God, they might be delivered from the Philistines. Ministers would profit their people more if they did but pray more for them. <div eID="gen5366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5367" type="x-p"/> 2. They obey his summons, and not only come to the meeting, but conform to the intentions of it, and appear there very well disposed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.6">v. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen5367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5368" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">They drew water and poured it out before the Lord,</hi> signifying, [1.] Their humiliation and contrition for sin, owning themselves as water spilt upon the ground, which cannot be gathered up again (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.14">2 Sam. xiv. 14</reference>), so mean, so miserable, before God, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Ps. xxii. 14</reference>. The Chaldee reads it, <hi type="italic">They poured out their hearts in repentance before the Lord.</hi> They wept rivers of tears, and sorrowed after a godly sort, for it was before the Lord and with an eye to him. [2.] Their earnest prayers and supplications to God for mercy. The soul is, in prayer, poured out before God, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.8">Ps. lxii. 8</reference>. [3.] Their universal reformation; they thus expressed their willingness to part with all their sins, and to retain no more of the relish or savour of them than the vessel does of the water that is poured out of it. They were free and full in their confession, and fixed in their resolution to cast away from them <hi type="italic">all their transgressions.</hi> Israel is now <hi type="italic">baptized from their idols,</hi> so Dr. Lightfoot. [4.] Some think it signifies their joy in the hope of God's mercy, which Samuel had assured them of. This ceremony was used with that signification at the feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="John.7.37-John.7.38">John vii. 37, 38</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Isa. xii. 3</reference>. Taking it in this sense, it must be read, <hi type="italic">They drew water after they had fasted.</hi> In the close of their humiliation they thus expressed their hope of pardon and reconciliation. <div eID="gen5368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5369" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">They fasted,</hi> abstained from food, afflicted their souls, so expressing repentance and exciting devotion. <div eID="gen5369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5370" type="x-p"/> (3.) They made a public confession: <hi type="italic">We have sinned against the Lord,</hi> so giving glory to God and taking shame to themselves. And, if we thus confess our sins, we shall find our God <hi type="italic">faithful and just to forgive us our sins.</hi> <div eID="gen5370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5371" type="x-p"/> 3. Samuel judged them at that time in Mizpeh, that is, he assured them, in God's name, of the pardon of their sins, upon their repentance, and that God was reconciled to them. It was a judgment of absolution. Or he received informations against those that did not leave their idols, and proceeded against them according to law. Those that would not judge themselves he judged. Or now he settled courts of justice among them, and appointed the terms and circuits which he observed afterwards, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.16">v. 16</reference>. Now he set those wheels a-going; and, whereas he began to act as a magistrate, to prevent their relapsing into those sins which now they seemed to have renounced.
entries.17973f8f5a5ad4e9deb2b9e2da421e683eac50ee: <div eID="gen5371" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Israelites Attacked by the Philistines; Samuel's Intercession for Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1099.)</title> <div sID="gen5372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And when the Philistines heard that the children of Israel were gathered together to Mizpeh, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the children of Israel heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they were afraid of the Philistines. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the children of Israel said to Samuel, Cease not to cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Samuel took a sucking lamb, and offered <hi type="italic">it for</hi> a burnt offering wholly unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and Samuel cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for Israel; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> heard him. <hi type="super">10</hi> And as Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to battle against Israel: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them; and they were smitten before Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the men of Israel went out of Mizpeh, and pursued the Philistines, and smote them, until <hi type="italic">they came</hi> under Beth-car. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then Samuel took a stone, and set <hi type="italic">it</hi> between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> helped us. <div eID="gen5372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5373" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The Philistines invade Israel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.7">v. 7</reference>), taking umbrage from that general meeting for repentance and prayer as if it had been a rendezvous for war, and, if so, they thought it prudent to keep the war out of their own country. They had no just cause for this suspicion; but those that seek to do mischief to others will be forward to imagine that others design mischief to them. Now see here, 1. How evil sometimes seems to come out of good. The religious meeting of the Israelites at Mizpeh brought trouble upon them from the Philistines, which perhaps tempted them to wish they had staid at home and to blame Samuel for calling them together. But we may be in God's way and yet meet with distress; nay, when sinners begin to repent and reform, they must expect that Satan will muster all his force against them, and set his instruments on work to the utmost to oppose and discourage them. But, 2. How good is, at length, brought out of that evil. Israel could never be threatened more seasonably than at this time, when they were repenting and praying, nor could they have been better prepared to receive the enemy; nor could the Philistines have acted more impolitely for themselves than to make war upon Israel at this time, when they were making their peace with God. But God permitted them to do it, that he might have an opportunity immediately of crowning his people's reformation with tokens of his favour, and of confirming the words of his messenger, who had assured them that if they repented God would <hi type="italic">deliver them out of the hand of the Philistines.</hi> Thus he makes man's wrath to praise him, and serves the purposes of his grace to his people even by the malicious designs of their enemies against them, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen5373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5374" type="x-p"/> II. Israel cleaves closely to Samuel, as their best friend, under God, in this distress; though he was no military man, nor ever celebrated as a mighty man of valour, yet, being afraid of the Philistines, for whom they thought themselves an unequal match, they engaged Samuel's prayers for them: <hi type="italic">Cease not to cry unto the Lord our God for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.8">v. 8</reference>. They were here unarmed, unprepared for war, come together to fast and pray, not to fight; prayers and tears therefore being all the weapons many of them are now furnished with, to these they have recourse. And, knowing Samuel to have a great interest in heaven, they earnestly beg of him to improve it for them. They had reason to expect it, because he had promised to <hi type="italic">pray for them</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">v. 5</reference>), had promised them deliverance from the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">v. 3</reference>), and they had been observant of him in all that which he had spoken to them from the Lord. Thus those who sincerely submit to Christ, as their lawgiver and judge, need not doubt of their interest in his intercession. They were very solicitous that Samuel should not cease to pray for them: what military preparations were to be made they would undertake them, but let him continue instant in prayer, perhaps remembering that when Moses did but let down his hand ever so little Amalek prevailed. O what a comfort is it to all believers that our great intercessor above never ceases, is never silent, for he <hi type="italic">always appears in the presence of God for us!</hi> <div eID="gen5374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5375" type="x-p"/> III. Samuel intercedes with God for them, and does it <hi type="italic">by sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.9">v. 9</reference>. He took a sucking lamb, and offered it for a <hi type="italic">burnt-offering, a whole burnt-offering, to the Lord,</hi> and, while the sacrifice was in burning, with the smoke of it his prayers ascended up to heaven for Israel. Observe, 1. He made intercession with a sacrifice. Christ intercedes in the virtue of his satisfaction, and in all our prayers we must have an eye to his great oblation, depending upon that for audience and acceptance. Samuel's sacrifice without his prayer would have been an empty shadow, his prayer without the sacrifice would not have been so prevalent, but both together teach us what great things we may expect from God in answer to those prayers which are made with faith in Christ's sacrifice. 2. It was a burnt-offering, which was offered purely for the glory of God, so intimating that the great plea he relied on in his prayer was taken from the honour of God. "Lord, help thy people now for thy name's sake." When we endeavour to give glory to God we may hope he will, in answer to our prayers, work for his own glory. 3. It was but one sucking lamb that he offered; for it is the integrity and intention of the heart that God looks at, more than the bulk or number of the offerings. This one lamb (typifying the Lamb of God) was more acceptable than thousands of rams or bullocks would have been without faith and prayer. Samuel was no priest, but he was a Levite and a prophet; the case was extraordinary, and what he did was by special direction, and therefore was accepted of God. And justly was this reproach put upon the priests because they had corrupted themselves. <div eID="gen5375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5376" type="x-p"/> IV. God gave a gracious answer to Samuel's prayer (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord heard him.</hi> He was himself a <hi type="italic">Samuel, asked of God,</hi> and many a Samuel, many a mercy in answer to prayer, God gave him. Sons of prayer should be famous for praying, as <hi type="italic">Samuel was among those that call upon his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Ps. xcix. 6</reference>. The answer was a real answer: the Philistines were discomfited (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10-1Sam.7.11">v. 10, 11</reference>), totally routed, and that in such a manner as highly magnified the prayer of Samuel, the power of God, and the valour of Israel. 1. The prayer of Samuel was honoured; for at the very time when he was offering up his sacrifice, and his prayer with it, the battle began, and turned immediately against the Philistines. Thus <hi type="italic">while he was yet speaking God heard,</hi> and answered in thunder, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa. lxv. 24</reference>. God showed that it was Samuel's prayer and sacrifice that he had respect to, and hereby let Israel know that as in a former engagement with the Philistines he had justly chastised their presumptuous confidence in the presence of the ark, on the shoulders of two profane priests, so now he graciously accepted their humble dependence upon the prayer of faith from the mouth and heart of a pious prophet. 2. The power of God was greatly honoured; for he took the work into his own hand, and discomfited them, not with great hail-stones, which would kill them (as <reference osisRef="Josh.10.11">Josh. x. 11</reference>), but with a great thunder, which frightened them and put them into such terror and consternation that they fainted away, and became a very easy prey to the sword of Israel, before whom, being thus confounded, they were smitten. Josephus adds that the earth quaked under them when first they made the onset and in many places opened and swallowed them up, and that, besides the terror of the thunder, their faces and hands were burnt with lightning, which obliged them to shift for themselves by flight. And, being thus driven to their heels by the immediate hand of God (whom they feared not so much as they had feared his ark, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>), then, 3. Honour was put upon the hosts of Israel; they were made use of for the completing of the victory, and had the pleasure of triumphing over their oppressors: <hi type="italic">They pursued the Philistines, and smote them.</hi> How soon did they find the benefit of their repentance, and reformation, and return to God! Now that they have thus engaged him for them none of their enemies can stand before them. <div eID="gen5376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5377" type="x-p"/> V. Samuel erected a thankful memorial of this victory, to the glory of God and for the encouragement of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.12">v. 12</reference>. He set up an <hi type="italic">Eben-ezer, the stone of help.</hi> If ever the people's hard hearts should lose the impressions of this providence, this stone would either revive the remembrance of it, and make them thankful, or remain a standing witness against them for their unthankfulness. 1. The place where this memorial was set up was the same where, twenty years before, the Israelites were smitten before the Philistines, for that was beside Eben-ezer, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1">ch. iv. 1</reference>. The sin which procured that defeat formerly being pardoned upon their repentance, the pardon was sealed by this glorious victory in the very same place where they then suffered loss; see <reference osisRef="Hos.1.10">Hos. i. 10</reference>. 2. Samuel himself took care to set up this monument. He had been instrumental by prayer to obtain the mercy, and therefore he thought himself in a special manner obliged to make this grateful acknowledgement of it. 3. The reason he gives for the name is, <hi type="italic">Hitherto the Lord hath helped us,</hi> in which he speaks thankfully of what was past, giving the glory of the victory to God only, who had added this to all his former favours; and yet he speaks somewhat doubtfully for the future: "Hitherto things have done well, but what God may yet do with us we know not, <hi type="italic">that</hi> we refer to him; but let us praise him for what he has done." Note, The beginnings of mercy and deliverance are to be acknowledged by us with thankfulness so far as they go, though they be not completely finished, nay, though the issue seem uncertain. <hi type="italic">Having obtained help from God, I continue hitherto,</hi> says blessed Paul, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.22">Acts xxvi. 22</reference>.
entries.fe59c54deb3210549733a52902fd31af44a7e12e: <div eID="gen5377" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Defeat of the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1092.)</title> <div sID="gen5378" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> So the Philistines were subdued, and they came no more into the coast of Israel: and the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the cities which the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron even unto Gath; and the coasts thereof did Israel deliver out of the hands of the Philistines. And there was peace between Israel and the Amorites. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he went from year to year in circuit to Bethel, and Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places. <hi type="super">17</hi> And his return <hi type="italic">was</hi> to Ramah; for there <hi type="italic">was</hi> his house; and there he judged Israel; and there he built an altar unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen5378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5379" type="x-p"/> We have here a short account of the further good services that Samuel did to Israel. Having parted them from their idols, and brought them home to their God, he had put them into a capacity of receiving further benefits by his ministry. Having prevailed in that, he becomes, in other instances, a great blessing to them; yet, writing it himself, he is brief in the relation. We are not told here, but it appears (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.18">2 Chron. xxxv. 18</reference>) that in the days of Samuel the prophet the people of Israel kept the ordinance of the passover with more than ordinary devotion, notwithstanding the distance of the ark and the desolations of Shiloh. Many good offices, no doubt, he did for Israel, but here we are only told how instrumental he was, 1. In securing the public peace (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In his days the Philistines came no more into the coast of Israel,</hi> made no inroads or incursions upon them; they perceived that God now fought for Israel and that his hand was against the Philistines, and this kept them in awe, and restrained the remainder of their wrath." Samuel was a protector and deliverer to Israel, not by dint of sword, as Gideon, nor by strength of arm, as Samson, but by the power of prayer to God and carrying on a work of reformation among the people. Religion and piety are the best securities of a nation. 2. In recovering the public rights, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.14">v. 14</reference>. By his influence Israel had the courage to demand the cities which the Philistines had unjustly taken from them and had long detained; and the Philistines, not daring to contend with one that had so great an interest in heaven, tamely yielded to the demand, and restored (some think) even Ekron and Gath, two of the capital cities, though afterwards they retook them; others think some small towns that lay between Ekron and Gath, which were forced out of the Philistines' hands. This they got by their reformation and religion, they got ground of their enemies and got forward in their affairs. It is added, <hi type="italic">There was peace between Israel and the Amorites,</hi> that is, the Canaanites, the remains of the natives. Not that Israel made any league with them, but they were quiet, and not so mischievous to Israel as they had sometimes been. Thus <hi type="italic">when a man's ways please the Lord he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him</hi> and give him no disturbance, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.7">Prov. xvi. 7</reference>. 3. In administering public justice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.15-1Sam.7.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">He judged Israel;</hi> as a prophet he taught them their duty and reproved them for their sins, which is called <hi type="italic">judging,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.4">Ezek. xx. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.2">xxii. 2</reference>. Moses judged Israel when he <hi type="italic">made them know the statutes of God and his laws</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.16">Exod. xviii. 16</reference>); and thus Samuel judged them to the last, even after Saul was made king; so he promised them then, when Saul was inaugurated (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.23">ch. xii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will</hi> not cease to <hi type="italic">teach you the good and the right way.</hi> As a magistrate, he received appeals from the inferior courts and gave judgment upon them, tried causes and determined them, tried prisoners and acquitted or condemned them, according to the law. This he did all his days, till he grew old and past service, and resigned to Saul; and afterwards he exercised authority when application was made to him; nay, he judged even Agag, and Saul himself. But when he was in his prime he rode the circuit, for the convenience of the country, at least of that part of it which lay most under his influence. He kept courts at Beth-el, Gilgal, and Mizpeh, all in the tribe of Benjamin; but his constant residence was at Ramah, his father's city, and there he judged Israel, thither they resorted to him from all parts with their complaints, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.17">v. 17</reference>. 4. In keeping up the public exercises of religion; for there, where he lived, he built an altar to the Lord, not in contempt of the altar that was at Nob, or Gibeon, or wherever the tabernacle was; but divine justice having laid Shiloh waste, and no other place being yet chosen for them to bring their offerings to (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">Deut. xii. 11</reference>), he looked upon the law which confined them to one place to be for the present suspended, and therefore, being a prophet, and under divine direction, he did as the patriarchs did, he built an altar where he lived, both for the use of his own family and for the good of the country that resorted to it. Great men should use their wealth, power, and interest, for the keeping up of religion in the places where they live.  <chapter eID="1Sam.7"/> <div eID="gen5379" type="x-p"/>

entries.ceaa08f71aabcb2d5ff4e1cb310af79edbc6fe95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2554"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <div sID="gen3454" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1">1Sa 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">2</reference>. The Ark at Kirjath-jearim.<div eID="gen3454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2554"/><hi type="bold">1. the men of Kirjath-jearim--</hi>"the city of woods," also Kirjath-baal (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.60">Jos 15:60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.14">18:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.5">1Ch 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.6">6</reference>). It was the nearest town to Beth-shemesh and stood on a hill. This was the reason of the message (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.21">1Sa 6:21</reference>), and why this was chosen for the convenience of people turning their faces to the ark (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.29-1Kgs.8.35">1Ki 8:29-35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Da 6:10</reference>).<div eID="gen3455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill--</hi>Why it was not transported at once to Shiloh where the tabernacle and sacred vessels were remaining, is difficult to conjecture.<div eID="gen3456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctified ... his son--</hi>He was not a Levite, and was therefore only set apart or appointed to be keeper of the place. <div eID="gen3457" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc2ab17f06f8199574c62f0c5b4980369f6e7da0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2555"/><div sID="gen3458" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2555"/><hi type="bold">2. the ark abode in Kirjath-jearim ... twenty years--</hi>It appears, in the subsequent history, that a much longer period elapsed before its final removal from Kirjath-jearim (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.19">2Sa 6:1-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.1-1Chr.13.14">1Ch 13:1-14</reference>). But that length of time had passed when the Israelites began to revive from their sad state of religious decline. The capture of the ark had produced a general indifference either as to its loss or its recovery.<div eID="gen3458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord--</hi>They were then brought, doubtless by the influence of Samuel's exhortations, to renounce idolatry, and to return to the national worship of the true God.<div eID="gen3459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3460" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3-1Sam.7.6">1Sa 7:3-6</reference>. The Israelites, through Samuel's Influence, Solemnly Repent at Mizpeh. <div eID="gen3460" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0eacb829d03223cb45709783ba1da0babdce056: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2556"/><div sID="gen3461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2556"/><hi type="bold">3-6. Samuel spake unto all the house of Israel--</hi>A great national reformation was effected through the influence of Samuel. Disgusted with their foreign servitude, and panting for the restoration of liberty and independence, they were open to salutary impressions; and convinced of their errors, they renounced idolatry. The re-establishment of the faith of their fathers was inaugurated at a great public meeting, held at Mizpeh in Judah, and hallowed by the observance of impressive religious solemnities. The drawing water, and pouring it out before the Lord, seems to have been a symbolical act by which, in the people's name, Samuel testified their sense of national corruption, their need of that moral purification of which water is the emblem, and their sincere desire to pour out their hearts in repentance before God. <div eID="gen3461" type="x-p"/>
entries.71288ed0b31395ba57e8b5cde92744aa88591de3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2558"/><div sID="gen3464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2558"/><hi type="bold">7-11. when the Philistines heard, &c.--</hi>The character and importance of the national convention at Mizpeh were fully appreciated by the Philistines. They discerned in it the rising spirit of religious patriotism among the Israelites that was prepared to throw off the yoke of their domination. Anxious to crush it at the first, they made a sudden incursion while the Israelites were in the midst of their solemn celebration. Unprepared for resistance, they besought Samuel to supplicate the divine interposition to save them from their enemies. The prophet's prayers and sacrifice were answered by such a tremendous storm of thunder and lightning that the assailants, panic-struck, were disordered and fled. The Israelites, recognizing the hand of God, rushed courageously on the foe they had so much dreaded and committed such immense havoc, that the Philistines did not for long recover from this disastrous blow. This brilliant victory secured peace and independence to Israel for twenty years, as well as the restitution of the usurped territory. <div eID="gen3464" type="x-p"/>
entries.3981587d81615ecc1b6558d2699cfea6fd5fb795: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2559"/><div sID="gen3465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2559"/><hi type="bold">12. Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen--</hi>on an open spot between the town and "the crag" (some well-known rock in the neighborhood). A huge stone pillar was erected as a monument of their victory (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Le 26:1</reference>). The name--Eben-ezer--is thought to have been written on the face of it. <chapter eID="1Sam.7"/>

entries.48859d2a9acc9bd207747800c598d4f402798649: <div eID="gen9784" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9785" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9786" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9786" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9785" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9787" type="x-p"/> The men of Kirjah-jearim bring the ark from Beth-shemesh, and consecrate Eleazar, the son of Abinadab, to keep it; and there it continued twenty years, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1">1Sam 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1Sam 7:2</reference>. Samuel reproves and exhorts the people, and gathers them together at Mizpeh, where they fast and pray, and confess their sins, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3-1Sam.7.6">1Sam 7:3-6</reference>. The Philistines go up against them; the Israelites cry unto the Lord for help; Samuel offers sacrifices; and the Lord confounds the Philistines with thunder; Israel discomfits and pursues them to Beth-car, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.7-1Sam.7.11">1Sam 7:7-11</reference>. Samuel erects a stone for a memorial, and calls it Eben-ezer, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.12">1Sam 7:12</reference>. The Philistines are totally subdued, and Israel recovers all its lost cities, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13">1Sam 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.14">1Sam 7:14</reference>. Samuel acts as an itinerant judge in Israel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.15-1Sam.7.17">1Sam 7:15-17</reference>. <div eID="gen9787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9788" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9789" type="x-p"/> Fetched up the ark - When these people received the message of the Beth-shemites, they probably consulted Samuel, with whom was the counsel of the Lord, and he had encouraged them to go and bring it up, else they might have expected such destruction as happened to the Beth-shemites. <div eID="gen9789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9790" type="x-p"/> Sanctified Eleazar - Perhaps this sanctifying signifies no more than setting this man apart, simply to take care of the ark.
entries.a4e655eb2723b5061e1e0694a390cbf97bced87a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9791" type="x-p"/> It was twenty years - This chapter contains the transactions of at least twenty years, but we know not the date of each event.
entries.5eb0b1f2fc075b5fbda9e1d099cc54e9ae8474ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9792" type="x-p"/> And Samuel spake - We have heard nothing of this judge since he served in the tabernacle. He was now grown up, and established for a prophet in the land of Israel. <div eID="gen9792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9793" type="x-p"/> If ye do return - From your backsliding and idolatry. <div eID="gen9793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9794" type="x-p"/> With all your hearts - For outward services and professions will avail nothing. <div eID="gen9794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9795" type="x-p"/> Put away the strange gods - Destroy their images, altars, and groves: they are strange; you do not know them as helpers, saviours, or defenders. <div eID="gen9795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9796" type="x-p"/> Prepare your hearts - Let your hearts be straight and steady. <div eID="gen9796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9797" type="x-p"/> And serve him only - Have no other religious service but his, and obey his laws. <div eID="gen9797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9798" type="x-p"/> He will deliver you - Vain are your own exertions; he will deliver you in such a way as to show that the excellence of the power is of himself alone.
entries.87c8cbc3c7af379af9c831208ea70b7ebb3ad53f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9799" type="x-p"/> Put away Baalim and Ashtaroth - These were not two particular deities, but two genera of idols; the one masculine, Baalim; the other feminine, Ashtaroth; both the words are in the plural number, and signify all their gods and goddesses.
entries.3bd028608c9ab63f2164abc5a8aa40737f717a5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9800" type="x-p"/> Gather all Israel to Mizpeh - This appears to have been an armed assembly, though probably collected principally for religious and political purposes; but Samuel knew that an unarmed multitude could not safely be convened in the vicinity of the Philistines.
entries.d9c87964c4ad3994ebed7563e65ccc82a77ac17e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen9800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9801" type="x-p"/> Drew water, and poured it out - It is not easy to know what is meant by this; it is true that pouring out water, in the way of libation, was a religious ordinance among the Hebrews, (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Isa 12:3</reference>), and among most other nations, particularly the Greeks and Romans, who used, not only water, but wine, milk, honey, and blood, as we find by Homer, Virgil, Euripides, Sophocles, Porphyry, and Lucian. Our Lord seems to allude to this ceremony, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.37-Joh.7.38">Joh 7:37-38</reference> (note), where see the note. <div eID="gen9801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9802" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee Paraphrast understands the place differently, for he translates: "And they poured out their hearts in penitence, as Waters, before the Lord." That deep penitential sorrow was represented under the notion of pouring out water, we have a direct proof in the case of David, who says, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.14">Psa 22:14</reference>, I am Poured Out like Water, my heart is like wax; it is Melted in the midst of my bowels. And to repentance, under this very similitude, the prophet exhorts fallen Jerusalem: Arise, cry out in the night; in the beginning of the watches Pour Out thine Heart Like Water before the face of the Lord; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">Lam 2:19</reference>. David uses the same image, <reference osisRef="Psa.62.8">Psa 62:8</reference> : Trust in him at all times, ye people; Pour Out your hearts before him. The same figure is used by Hannah in <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.15">1Sam 1:15</reference> of this book; I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have Poured Out my soul before the Lord. Perhaps the drawing and pouring out of water mentioned in the text was done emblematically, to represent the contrition of their hearts. <div eID="gen9802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9803" type="x-p"/> And Samuel judged - He gave them ordinances, heard and redressed grievances, and taught them how to get reconciled to God. The assembly, therefore, was held for religio-politico-military purposes.
entries.dc44cc5725c898e9a1ca6e9b934a5cf23ffa5148: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9804" type="x-p"/> The Philistines went up against Israel - They went to give them battle before that, by continual accessions of numbers, they should become too powerful.
entries.d5e106957f19a044612c0d8593ef894a480783b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9805" type="x-p"/> Cease not to cry unto the Lord - They had strong confidence in the intercession of Samuel, because they knew he was a holy man of God.
entries.c40e8390f5cbf458c1a18644f15e3ce4fa32b7e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen9805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9806" type="x-p"/> Samuel took a sucking lamb - This sucking lamb must have been eight days under its mother before it could be offered, as the law says, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.27">Lev 22:27</reference>. <div eID="gen9806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9807" type="x-p"/> Though Samuel was not a priest, yet he offered this sacrifice; or he might have ordered Eleazar to offer it, and still be said to have done it himself: Qui facit per alterum, facit per se; "He who procures a thing to be done, may be said to do it himself." His not sacrificing at the tabernacle was justified by the necessity of the case; neither tabernacle nor ark was at hand.
entries.f93b1495ff57d43b6ba7c08a1f2c52874c7d6171: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9808" type="x-p"/> The Lord thundered with a great thunder - Literally, The Lord thundered with a great voice - he confounded them with a mighty tempest of thunder and lightning, and no doubt slew many by the lightning.
entries.908d57cf69dfd6104794d23bf8574f35bd758f36: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen9808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9809" type="x-p"/> Under Beth-car - We know not where this place was; the Septuagint have Beth-chor; the Targum, Beth-saron; and the Syriac and Arabic, Beth-jasan.
entries.7c17e2d78b5623932d6ea11eab2d63e675b5e05c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9810" type="x-p"/> Called the name of it Eben-ezer - אבן העזר Eben haezer, "The Stone of Help;" perhaps a pillar is meant by the word stone.
entries.ca73f91deace07b3cc15d7b3a82356d71db00214: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9811" type="x-p"/> They came no more into the coast of Israel - Perhaps a more signal victory was never gained by Israel; the Lord had brought them low, almost to extermination; and now, by his miraculous interference, he lifts them completely up, and humbles to the dust their proud oppressors. God often suffers nations and individuals to be brought to the lowest extremity, that he may show his mercy and goodness by suddenly rescuing them from destruction, when all human help has most evidently failed.
entries.ae79d0ce122f609f3dc68b4bf8c2933f84653776: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen9811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9812" type="x-p"/> The cities which the Philistines had taken - We are not informed of the particulars of these reprisals, but we may rest assured all this was not done in one day: perhaps the retaking of the cities was by slow degrees, through the space of several years. <div eID="gen9812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9813" type="x-p"/> There was peace between Israel and the Amorites - That is, all the remaining Canaanites kept quiet, and did not attempt to molest the Israelites, when they found the Philistines, the most powerful of the ancient inhabitants of the land, broken and subdued before them.
entries.af0b9a791fccabe482bc2b3e75d5ab7b5697201d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen9813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9814" type="x-p"/> Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life - Samuel is supposed to have lived one hundred years; he did not begin to judge Israel till he was about forty years of age; and if he was one hundred years of age when he died, he must have been a judge sixty years, and consequently filled that office during the whole of Saul's reign. But that he had been dead before Saul's last battle, is evident from the transactions of that king with the witch of En-dor, and probably not long before. Samuel was the prophet of that time; declared the will of the Lord, and frequently directed both the civil and military transactions of the kingdom. Samuel seems, in many respects, to have been considered the governor of the people, while Saul was only looked on as the general of the armies.
entries.8914c2178625c0997e9315efed8d4c02f3ce6c68: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen9814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9815" type="x-p"/> He went from year to year in circuit - When he was at Beth-el, the tribe of Ephraim, and all the northern parts of the country, could attend him; when at Gilgal, the tribe of Benjamin, and those beyond Jordan, might have easy access to him; and when at Mizpeh, he was within reach of Judah, Simeon, and Gad; but Ramah was the place of his ordinary abode; and there he held his court, for there he judged Israel; and, as it is probable that Shiloh was destroyed, it is said, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.17">1Sam 7:17</reference>, that there (viz., at Ramah) he built an altar unto the Lord. This altar, being duly consecrated, the worship performed at it was strictly legal. Ramah, which is said to be about six miles from Jerusalem, was the seat of prophecy during the life of Samuel; and there it is probable all Israel came to consult him on matters of a spiritual nature, as there was the only altar of God in the land of Israel.  <chapter eID="1Sam.7"/> <div eID="gen9815" type="x-p"/>

entries.eee8007f51b6cf34976e0e5f71fec124e1bdf156: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.1">1Sa 7:1</reference> <div eID="gen3740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3741" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Kirjath-jearim complied with this request, and brought the ark into the house of Abinadab upon the height, and sanctified Abinadab’s son Eleazar to be the keeper of the ark. <hi type="italic">Kirjath-jearim</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Kuryet el Enab</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>), was neither a priestly nor a Levitical city. The reason why the ark was taken there, is to be sought for, therefore, in the situation of the town, i.e., in the fact that Kirjath-jearim was the nearest large town on the road from Bethshemesh to Shiloh. We have no definite information, however, as to the reason why it was not taken on to Shiloh, to be placed in the tabernacle, but was allowed to remain in the house of Abinadab at Kirjath-jearim, where a keeper was expressly appointed to take charge of it; so that we can only confine ourselves to conjectures. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>'s opinion (<hi type="italic">Gesch. </hi>ii. 540), that the Philistines had conquered Shiloh after the victory described in 1 Samuel 4, and had destroyed the ancient sanctuary there, i.e., the tabernacle, is at variance with the accounts given in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.6">1Sa 21:6</reference>; 1Ki 3:4; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2Ch 1:3</reference>, respecting the continuance of worship in the tabernacle at Nob and Gibeon. There is much more to be said in support of the conjecture, that the carrying away of the ark by the Philistines was regarded as a judgment upon the sanctuary, which had been desecrated by the reckless conduct of the sons of Eli, and consequently, that even when the ark itself was recovered, they would not take it back without an express declaration of the will of God, but were satisfied, as a temporary arrangement, to leave the ark in Kirjath-jearim, which was farther removed from the cities of the Philistines. And there it remained, because no declaration of the divine will followed respecting its removal into the tabernacle, and the tabernacle itself had to be removed from Shiloh to Nob, and eventually to Gibeon, until David had effected the conquest of the citadel of Zion, and chosen Jerusalem as his capital, when it was removed from Kirjath-jearim to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). It is not stated that Abinadab was a Levites; but this is very probable, because otherwise they would hardly have consecrated his son to be the keeper of the ark, but would have chosen a Levite for the office.
entries.ea2d1aa2a5cb5179f78b29e51c301ddbc2e1fe57: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2-1Sam.7.4">1Sa 7:2-4</reference> <hi type="italic">Purification of Israel from idolatry</hi>. - Twenty years passed away from that time forward, while the ark remained at Kirjath-jearim, and all Israel mourned after Jehovah. Then Samuel said to them, “<hi type="italic">If ye turn to the Lord with all your heart, put away the strange gods from the midst of you, and the Astartes, and direct your heart firmly upon the Lord, and serve Him only, that He may save you out of the hand of the Philistines</hi>.” And the Israelites listened to this appeal. The single clauses of <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1Sa 7:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">1Sa 7:3</reference> are connected together by <hi type="italic">vav consec</hi>., and are not to be separated from one another. There is no gap between these verses; but they contain the same closely and logically connected thought,<note placement="foot">There is no force at all in the proofs which Thenius has adduced of a gap between <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1Sa 7:2</reference> and 1Sa 7:3. It by no means follows, that because the Philistines had brought back the ark, their rule over the Israelites had ceased, so as to make the words “he will deliver you,” etc., incomprehensible. Moreover, the appearance of Samuel as <hi type="italic">judge</hi> does not presuppose that his assumption of this office must necessarily have been mentioned before. As a general rule, there was no such formal assumption of the office, and this would be least of all the case with Samuel, who had been recognised as an accredited prophet of Jehovah (1Sa 3:19.). And lastly, the reference to idols, and to their being put away in consequence of Samuel’s appeal, is intelligible enough, without any express account of their falling into idolatry, if we bear in mind, on the one hand, the constant inclination of the people to serve other gods, and if we observe, on the other hand, that Samuel called upon the people to turn to the Lord with all their heart and serve Him alone, which not only does not preclude, but actually implies, the outward continuance of the worship of Jehovah.</note> which may be arranged in one period in the following manner: “And it came to pass, when the days multiplied from the time that the ark remained at Kirjath-jearim, and grew to twenty years, and the whole house of Israel mourned after Jehovah, that Samuel said,” etc. The verbs ויּרבּוּ, ויּהיוּ, and ויּנּהוּ, are merely continuations of the infinitive שׁבת, and the main sentence is resumed in the words שׁמוּאל ויּאמר. The contents of the verses require that the clauses should be combined in this manner. The statement that twenty years had passed can only be understood on the supposition that some kind of turning-point ensued at the close of that time. The complaining of the people after Jehovah was no such turning-point, but became one simply from the fact that this complaining was followed by some result. This result is described in 1Sa 7:3. It consisted in the fact that Samuel exhorted the people to put away the strange gods (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">1Sa 7:3</reference>); and that when the people listened to his exhortation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.4">1Sa 7:4</reference>), he helped them to gain a victory over the Philistines (1Sa 7:5.). ינּהוּ, from נהה, to lament or complain (Mic 2:4; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.18">Eze 32:18</reference>). “The phrase, <hi type="italic">to lament after God</hi>, is taken from human affairs, when one person follows another with earnest solicitations and complaints, until he at length assents. We have an example of this in the Syrophenician woman in Matt 15.” (Seb. Schmidt). The meaning “to assemble together,” which is the one adopted by <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, is forced upon the word from the Chaldee אתנהי, and it cannot be shown that the word was ever used in this sense in Hebrew. Samuel’s appeal in <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.3">1Sa 7:3</reference> recalls to mind <reference osisRef="Josh.24.14">Jos 24:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen 35:2</reference>; but the words, “<hi type="italic">If ye do return unto the Lord with all your hearts</hi>,” assume that the turning of the people to the Lord their God had already inwardly commenced, and indeed, as the participle שׁבים expresses duration, had commenced as a permanent thing, and simply demand that the inward turning of the heart to God should be manifested outwardly as well, by the putting away of all their idols, and should thus be carried out to completion. The “strange gods” (see <reference osisRef="Gen.35.2">Gen 35:2</reference>) are described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.4">1Sa 7:4</reference> as “<hi type="italic">Baalim</hi>.” On <hi type="italic">Baalim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi>, see at Jdg 2:11, Jdg 2:13. לב הכין, to direct the heart firmly: see <reference osisRef="Ps.78.8">Psa 78:8</reference>; 2Ch 30:19.<hi type="italic">Victory obtained over the Philistines through Samuel’s prayer</hi>. - <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">1Sa 7:5</reference>, 1Sa 7:6. When Israel had turned to the Lord with all its heart, and had put away all its idols, Samuel gathered together all the people at Mizpeh, to prepare them for fighting against the Philistines by a solemn day for penitence and prayer. For it is very evident that the object of calling all the people to Mizpeh was that the religious act performed there might serve as a consecration for battle, not only from the circumstance that, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.7">1Sa 7:7</reference>, when the Philistines heard of the meeting, they drew near to make war upon Israel, but also from the contents of <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">1Sa 7:5</reference> : “<hi type="italic">Samuel said</hi> (sc., to the heads or representatives of the nation), <hi type="italic">Gather all Israel to Mizpeh, and I will pray for you unto the Lord</hi>.” His intention could not possibly have been any other than to put the people into the right relation to their God, and thus to prepare the way for their deliverance out of the bondage of the Philistines. Samuel appointed <hi type="italic">Mizpeh</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Nebi Samwil</hi>, on the western boundary of the tribe of Benjamin (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.26">Jos 18:26</reference>), as the place of meeting, partly no doubt on historical grounds, viz., because it was there that the tribes had formerly held their consultations respecting the wickedness of the inhabitants of Gibeah, and had resolved to make war upon Benjamin (Jdg 20:1.), but still more no doubt, because Mizpeh, on the western border of the mountains, was the most suitable place for commencing the conflict with the Philistines.
entries.95ed897adac88351a982a3cbd590ec11a754bd74: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.6-1Sam.7.9">1Sa 7:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen3741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3742" type="x-p"/> When they had assembled together here, “<hi type="italic">they drew water and poured it out before Jehovah, and fasted on that day, and said there, We have sinned against the Lord</hi>.” Drawing water and pouring it out before Jehovah was a symbolical act, which has been thus correctly explained by the Chaldee, on the whole: “They poured out their heart like water in penitence before the Lord.” This is evident from the figurative expressions, “poured out like water,” in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">Psa 22:15</reference>, and “pour out thy heart like water,” in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">Lam 2:19</reference>, which are used to denote inward dissolution through pain, misery, and distress (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.14">2Sa 14:14</reference>). Hence the pouring out of water before God was a symbolical representation of the temporal and spiritual distress in which they were at the time, - a practical confession before God, “Behold, we are before Thee like water that has been poured out;” and as it was their own sin and rebellion against God that had brought this distress upon them, it was at the same time a confession of their misery, and an act of the deepest humiliation before the Lord. They gave a still further practical expression to this humiliation by fasting (צוּם), as a sign of their inward distress of mind on account of their sin, and an oral confession of their sin against the Lord. By the word שׁם, which is added to ויּאמרוּ, “they said “<hi type="italic">there</hi>,” i.e., at Mizpeh, the oral confession of their sin is formally separated from the two symbolical acts of humiliation before God, though by this very separation it is practically placed on a par with them. What they did symbolically by the pouring out of water and fasting, they explained and confirmed by their verbal confession. שׁם is never an adverb of time signifying “<hi type="italic">then</hi>;” neither in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.5">Psa 14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Psa 132:17</reference>, nor Jdg 5:11. “<hi type="italic">And thus Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpeh</hi>.” ויּשׁפּט does not mean “he became judge” (Mich. and others), any more than “he punished every one according to his iniquity” (Thenius, after David Kimchi). Judging the people neither consisted in a censure pronounced by Samuel afterwards, nor in absolution granted to the penitent after they had made a confession of their sin, but in the fact that Samuel summoned the nation to Mizpeh to humble itself before Jehovah, and there secured for it, through his intercession, the forgiveness of its sin, and a renewal of the favour of its God, and thus restored the proper relation between Israel and its God, so that the Lord could proceed to vindicate His people’s rights against their foes. <div eID="gen3742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3743" type="x-p"/> When the Philistines heard of the gathering of the Israelites at Mizpeh (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.7">1Sa 7:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.8">1Sa 7:8</reference>), their princes went up against Israel to make war upon it; and the Israelites, in their fear of the Philistines, entreated Samuel, “<hi type="italic">Do not cease to cry for us to the Lord our God, that He may save us out of the hand of the Philistines</hi>.” 1Sa 7:9. “<hi type="italic">And Samuel took a milk-lamb</hi> (a lamb that was still sucking, probably, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.22.27">Lev 22:27</reference>, a lamb seven days old), <hi type="italic">and offered it whole as a burnt-offering to the Lord</hi>.” כּליל is used adverbially, according to its original meaning as an adverb, “<hi type="italic">whole</hi>.” The Chaldee has not given the word at all, probably because the translators regarded it as pleonastic, since every burnt-offering was consumed upon the altar whole, and consequently the word כּליל was sometimes used in a substantive sense, as synonymous with עולה (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.10">Deu 33:10</reference>; Ps. 51:21). But in the passage before us, כּליל is not synonymous with עולה, but simply affirms that the lamb was offered upon the altar without being cut up or divided. Samuel selected a young lamb for the burnt-offering, not “as being the purest and most innocent kind of sacrificial animal,” - for it cannot possibly be shown that very young animals were regarded as purer than those that were full-grown, - but as being the most suitable to represent the nation that had wakened up to new life through its conversion to the Lord, and was, as it were, new-born. For the burnt-offering represented the man, who consecrated therein his life and labour to the Lord. The sacrifice was the substratum for prayer. When Samuel offered it, he cried to the Lord for the children of Israel; and the Lord “<hi type="italic">answered</hi>,” i.e., granted, his prayer.
entries.b9f99c8cbdeb7f79dbc25c80003ed8a173b341ef: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10">1Sa 7:10</reference> <div eID="gen3743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3744" type="x-p"/> When the Philistines advanced during the offering of the sacrifice to fight against Israel, “<hi type="italic">Jehovah thundered with a great noise</hi>,” i.e., with loud peals, against the Philistines, and threw them into confusion, so that they were smitten before Israel. The thunder, which alarmed the Philistines and threw them into confusion (יהמּם, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>), was the answer of God to Samuel’s crying to the Lord.
entries.6a2e0f4e295ddb7e534e798c33ca3de308e04731: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.11">1Sa 7:11</reference> <div eID="gen3744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3745" type="x-p"/> As soon as they took to flight, the Israelites advanced from Mizpeh, and pursued and smote them to below <hi type="italic">Beth-car</hi>. The situation of this town or locality, which is only mentioned here, has not yet been discovered. Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. vi. 2, 2) has μέχρι Κοῤῥαίων.
entries.c41ccc67e6e609bc4570e93496b2f2f3e3c827b0: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.12">1Sa 7:12</reference> <div eID="gen3745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3746" type="x-p"/> As a memorial of this victory, Samuel placed a stone between Mizpeh and Shen, to which he gave the name of <hi type="italic">Eben-ha-ezer</hi>, i.e., stone of help, as a standing memorial that the Lord had thus far helped His people. The situation of <hi type="italic">Shen</hi> is also not known. The name <hi type="italic">Shen</hi> (i.e., tooth) seems to indicate a projecting point of rock (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1Sa 14:4</reference>), but may also signify a place situated upon such a point.
entries.4dde5ae1d6d41c9a22c3a45551a47267256886fe: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13">1Sa 7:13</reference> <div eID="gen3746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3747" type="x-p"/> Through this victory which was obtained by the miraculous help of God, the Philistines were so humbled, that they no more invaded the territory of Israel, i.e., with lasting success, as they had done before. This limitation of the words “<hi type="italic">they came no more</hi>” (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “they did not add again to come into the border of Israel”), is implied in the context; for the words which immediately follow, “<hi type="italic">and the hand of Jehovah was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel</hi>,” show that they made attempts to recover their lost supremacy, but that so long as Samuel lived they were unable to effect anything against Israel. This is also manifest from the successful battles fought by Saul (1 Samuel 13 and 14), when the Philistines had made fresh attempts to subjugate Israel during his reign. The defeats inflicted upon them by Saul also belong to the days of Samuel, who died but a very few years before Saul himself. Because of these battles which Saul fought with the Philistines, Lyra and Brentius understand the expression “all the days of Samuel” as referring not to the lifetime of Samuel, but simply to the duration of his official life as judge, viz., till the commencement of Saul’s reign. But this is at variance with <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.15">1Sa 7:15</reference>, where Samuel is said to have judged Israel all the days of his life. Seb. Schmidt has given, on the whole, the correct explanation of <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13">1Sa 7:13</reference> : “They came no more so as to obtain a victory and subdue the Israelites as before; yet they did return, so that the hand of the Lord was against them, i.e., so that they were repulsed with great slaughter, although they were not actually expelled, or the Israelites delivered from tribute and the presence of military garrisons, and that all the days that the judicial life of Samuel lasted, in fact all his life, since they were also smitten by Saul.”
entries.1c68db018a96eb631bf9fd6ffb265742ad6b5242: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.14">1Sa 7:14</reference> <div eID="gen3747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3748" type="x-p"/> In consequence of the defeat at Ebenezer, the Philistines were obliged to restore to the Israelites the cities which they had taken from them, “<hi type="italic">from Ekron to Gath</hi>.” This definition of the limits is probably to be understood as <hi type="italic">exclusive</hi>, i.e., as signifying that the Israelites received back their cities up to the very borders of the Philistines, measuring these borders from Ekron to Gath, and not that the Israelites received Ekron and Gath also. For although these chief cities of the Philistines had been allotted to the tribes of Judah and Dan in the time of Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.3-Josh.13.4">Jos 13:3-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.45-Josh.15.46">Jos 15:45-46</reference>), yet, notwithstanding the fact that Judah and Simeon conquered Ekron, together with Gaza and Askelon, after the death of Joshua (Jdg 1:18), the Israelites did not obtain any permanent possession. “<hi type="italic">And their territory</hi>” (coasts), i.e., the territory of the towns that were given back to Israel, not that of Ekron and Gath, “<hi type="italic">did Israel deliver out of the hands of the Philistines. And there was peace between Israel and the Amorites</hi>;” i.e., the Canaanitish tribes also kept peace with Israel after this victory of the Israelites over the Philistines, and during the time of Samuel. The Amorites are mentioned, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.10.6">Jos 10:6</reference>, as being the most powerful of the Canaanitish tribes, who had forced the Danites out of the plain into the mountains (Jdg 1:34-35).
entries.ed5da94a40071bf444f47349678bdf25571f1e91: <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.15-1Sam.7.17">1Sa 7:15-17</reference> <hi type="italic">Samuel’s judicial labours</hi>. - With the calling of the people to Mizpeh, and the victory at Ebenezer that had been obtained through his prayer, Samuel had assumed the government of the whole nation; so that his office as judge dates from his period, although he had laboured as prophet among the people from the death of Eli, and had thereby prepared the way for the conversion of Israel to the Lord. As his prophetic labours were described in general terms in <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.19-1Sam.3.21">1Sa 3:19-21</reference>, so are his labours as judge in the verses before us: viz., in <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.15">1Sa 3:15</reference> their duration, - “<hi type="italic">all the days of his life</hi>,” as his activity during Saul’s reign and the anointing of David (1 Samuel 15-16) sufficiently prove; and then in <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.16">1Sa 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.17">1Sa 3:17</reference> their general character, - “<hi type="italic">he went round from year to year</hi>” (וסבב serves as a more precise definition of והלך, he went and travelled round) <hi type="italic">to Bethel</hi>, i.e., Beitin (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.7.2">Jos 7:2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Gilgal, and Mizpeh</hi> (see at. <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.5">1Sa 3:5</reference>), and judged Israel at all these places. Which Gilgal is meant, whether the one situated in the valley of the Jordan (<reference osisRef="Josh.4.19">Jos 4:19</reference>), or the <hi type="italic">Jiljilia</hi> on the higher ground to the south-west of Shiloh (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.8.35">Jos 8:35</reference>), cannot be determined with perfect certainty. The latter is favoured partly by the order in which the three places visited by Samuel on his circuits occur, since according to this he probably went first of all from Ramah to Bethel, which was to the north-east, then farther north or north-west to Jiljilia, and then turning back went towards the south-east to Mizpeh, and returning thence to Ramah performed a complete circuit; whereas, if the Gilgal in the valley of the Jordan had been the place referred to, we should expect him to go there first of all from Ramah, and then towards the north-east to Bethel, and from that to the south-west to Mizpeh; and partly also by the circumstance that, according to 2Ki 2:1 and 2Ki 4:38, there was a school of the prophets at Jiljilia in the time of Elijah and Elisha, the founding of which probably dated as far back as the days of Samuel. If this conjecture were really a well-founded one, it would furnish a strong proof that it was in this place, and not in the Gilgal in the valley of the Jordan, that Samuel judged the people. But as this conjecture cannot be raised into a certainty, the evidence in favour of Jiljilia is not so conclusive as I myself formerly supposed (see also the remarks on <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14">1Sa 9:14</reference>). כּל־המּקומות את is grammatically considered an accusative, and is in apposition to את־ישׂראל, lit., <hi type="italic">Israel</hi>, viz., all the places named, i.e., Israel which inhabited all these places, and was to be found there. “<hi type="italic">And this return was to Ramah</hi>;” i.e., after finishing the annual circuit he returned to Ramah, where he had his house. There he judged Israel, and also built an altar to conduct the religious affairs of the nation. Up to the death of Eli, Samuel lived and laboured at Shiloh (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.21">1Sa 3:21</reference>). But when the ark was carried away by the Philistines, and consequently the tabernacle at Shiloh lost what was most essential to it as a sanctuary, and ceased at once to be the scene of the gracious presence of God, Samuel went to his native town Ramah, and there built an altar as the place of sacrifice for Jehovah, who had manifested himself to him.
